references.title: Optically-Accelerated AI Clusters Enabled by Interoperable Multi-Vendor OCSs: Use Cases
references.slides_title: Optically-Accelerated AI Clusters Enabled by Interoperable Multi-Vendor OCSs: Use Cases and Opportunities
references.summary: Proposed optical AI-cluster architecture combines packet switching, OCS, CPO and software control. The principal emerging applications are shared spare pools for recovery and topology adaptation to collective communication. Open models and coordinated software are prerequisites; the deck presents planned interoperability work rather than a production deployment report.

evidence.finding: CPO and OCS perform different functions. EPS retains packet routing while OCS changes physical connectivity at multiple possible network layers.
Shared spare resources can replace dedicated one-for-one protection; the SDN controller redirects optical paths around a failed leaf or accelerator.
Direct optical connections may bypass leaf or spine EPS to suit All-Reduce or All-to-All. Coordination with job orchestration and communication libraries is required.
Temporary disconnection during optical reconfiguration can disrupt RoCEv2. Traffic visibility and hardware/software co-design remain identified gaps.
A common OCP OCS YANG model is intended to remove vendor-specific controller translators. An OCP/IOWN-GF multi-vendor recovery demonstration is planned for OFC2027.

course_placement.reference_label: Optional 2026 Summit perspective: interoperable optical AI clusters
course_placement.learner_prompt: Compare two motives for reconfiguration: replacing a failed resource and matching an AI job’s communication pattern. What software must coordinate each?

course_placement.reference_label: CPO and OCS serve complementary roles

limitations: Do not describe the OFC2027 demonstration as completed in 2026.
Do not claim measured job speedups or recovery-time guarantees; the selected use-case slides are architectural proposals.
The deck claims YANG R1.0 released, while the Interfaces deck labels its specification v0.8; do not infer a single current revision from these presentations.

references.title: Standardizing OCS Interfaces for Seamless Integration
references.summary: Explains a common OCS management approach based on OpenConfig/YANG and gNMI, including capability discovery, connection intent and observed port state. It shows how a shared API can accommodate different OCS technologies and restoration behaviors while reusing existing network-management tools.

evidence.finding: Existing management facilities can be reused, with OCS-specific changes concentrated in forwarding control, configuration and monitoring. OpenConfig supports familiar tooling and streaming telemetry.
gNMI provides Get, Set and Subscribe operations over modeled configuration and state.

Common operations cover connection establishment, restoration behavior, capability discovery, connection status and port health. Devices differ in connectivity constraints, switching behavior and cold-boot recovery.
The model separates device capabilities and port state from controller-selected connection intent. This permits inspection of requested and actual connections together.
The presentation identifies the interface specification as v0.8, points to the public OCP repository, and requests YANG/OpenConfig contributors.

Do not imply every OCS supports arbitrary any-to-any, multicast, unidirectional operation, or the same reboot behavior.

references.title: Zero-Touch OCS Fabrics for AI Scale-Out Infrastructure at Hyperscale
references.summary: Presents the operating requirements for scalable OCS fabrics: automated device lifecycle, verified end-to-end topology, predictable optical performance and qualified manufacturing supply. Its strongest introductory lesson is that successful optical programming does not by itself prove the intended packet path.

evidence.finding: Operational state requires endpoint evidence because the OCS cross-connect does not inspect packets. Optical presence or cross-connect status alone cannot prove the intended peer.

Automation spans initial identity and credentials, topology qualification, continuing health, upgrades and recovery. gNMI, gNOI and gNSI require common behavior and service semantics as well as transport compatibility.
Distinct expected peer patterns expose cabling mistakes and permit parallel path qualification, improving on simple serial loopback checks.
A safe change sequence uses intent, prechecks, programming, validation and commit, with rollback and retained evidence on failure.
Mass-production processes, alternate supply and consistent insertion loss complement software conformance. The presenters call for an operator-ready lifecycle profile and shared conformance tests.

course_placement.learner_prompt: Explain why manufacturing consistency and a shared conformance suite both matter to multi-vendor adoption.

limitations: This talk supports operational requirements, not a documented count, size or measured performance of Oracle production OCS deployments.
Slide 12 presents vendor optical-loss data and link-budget compatibility examples; do not generalize them into universal product specifications or a complete end-to-end loss budget.
The operator-ready profile is a call to action; do not present it as an already mandatory OCP standard.
